To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have been able to image intact thylakoidal membranes at molecular resolution.
the surface of intact thylakoidal membranes can be imaged at molecular resolution and that photosynthetic membrane structure and function can be studied in situ on native, hydrated thylakoids.

(i) the lateral resolution of the scanning force microscope (SFM) is sufficiently high to resolve individual pigment–protein complexes in intact chloroplasts; and (ii) in situ SFM is a unique tool to investigate thylaloid structure and function at a molecular level.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of scanning force microscopy (SFM) for the investigation of the structure and function of biological systems at the molecular level.
the development and application of scanning probe microscopy (SPM) for the study of biological systems, in particular photosynthetic membranes.
the development and application of scanning probe microscopy to the study of photosynthetic membranes and the molecular organization of the photosynthetic apparatus.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the present work demonstrates a new approach to study the structure of intact photosynthetic thylakoid membrane.
the thylakoid membrane is a highly dynamic structure, which undergoes structural changes in response to environmental stimuli, and that the structural and functional changes are interrelated.
the chloroplast is a highly complex organelle, with a very high degree of compartmentalization and specialization of its membranes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have demonstrated the feasibility of imaging the intact thylacoids with the atomic force microscope and that we have shown how the technique can be used to investigate the structural changes associated with the unstacking of grana membranes.
we can image intact photosynthesising membranes at a resolution of 5 nm and that we can follow changes in their structure in situ.

it is possible to image intact photosystems in situ at a lateral resolution better than 3 nm and vertical resolution better than 0.3 nm, which allows direct determination of surface density of the photosystems.
The main takeaway from our work is that
scanning probe microscopy can be used to image intact photosystems in situ at molecular resolution.
the surface structure of the thylakoid membrane is very complex and dynamic, and that it can be resolved at the level of individual protein complexes.
it is possible to study the structure of intact chloroplast membranes in their native environment using SPM.
